**Subject: Take the building off the market and call me**

Denis,

I am writing this in English because I want no misunderstanding about what I am saying. I have started this email several times and stopped because I was too angry to put the sentences together properly. I am still angry. You need to understand that before anything else.

How could you put Papa’s building on the market without calling me first?

On Thursday, at six in the morning, a photographer from the agency walked into my bakery while I was shaping the baguettes. I had flour on my hands, my employee Karine was working, and we were starting our day like we always do. Then this stranger was there with his camera, in my shop, acting like everything had already been arranged.

He told me that “Mr. Denis” had told him I was okay with it.

Is that really what you said? That I agreed? Because I did not agree. I did not even know. I learned that the building was for sale from a photographer standing in my bakery at six in the morning. Afterwards, I went online and found the listing on Centris myself: $1,150,000, with an agent, as if this was just another property and I was just somebody who had to be managed.

Karine had to calm me down. I was embarrassed, Denis, and then I was even angrier that you had put me in that position in my own place of work. You could not pick up the phone, but you could arrange for an agency to send somebody into my shop.

That was a cowardly way to handle this. I am not saying that to insult you for pleasure. I am telling you honestly what your action looks like from here. You did not have the courage to speak to me yourself, so you let an agent and a photographer deliver the news.

This is the three-storey building on rue Saint-Hubert that Papa bought in 1979. The bakery is on the ground floor, with the two apartments above it. I have operated my business there for 31 years. Since Maman died in February 2026 and the estate was settled in August, the building belongs half to you and half to me. Whatever the paperwork allows you to do, that does not make you the only person whose decision matters.

After Maman’s funeral, you called me and said, “No rush, we decide together.”

Together, Denis. Your word, not mine.

We had just buried our mother. I believed you. I believed that even if we did not always see things the same way, you understood that we had to speak honestly before making a decision like this. Now I have to ask what that promise meant to you. Did it mean anything at all, or was it simply something easy to say on the phone from Calgary?

I have paid $2,400 a month in rent to the estate, and I have never been late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 myself for the new roof. I did not do that so I could throw it back in your face years later. I did it because the roof needed to be replaced and because the building houses my business. But that was real money, and you cannot pretend I have contributed nothing except sentiment.

I also told you by phone in September that I wanted to buy your half. The caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. I was not speaking vaguely about perhaps doing something someday. I had already taken steps to find out what financing I could obtain. The exact price and structure would have to be discussed, of course, but you knew my intention was serious.

Instead of sitting down with me, getting an independent valuation, and discussing a fair way to do this, you listed the building behind my back.

You probably think I am being sentimental. I can almost hear you saying it. But this is business too. I have six employees whose jobs depend on that bakery. I have 31 years of work, clients, relationships, and reputation in that location. This is not something I can replace by putting my ovens in a truck and finding another storefront next week.

If a developer buys the building, we both know what can happen. They will tear it down, turn it into condos, or double my rent until I have no choice but to leave. I cannot survive that. A developer will not care how many years I have been there or how many people depend on me. They will look at the numbers, and I will be the inconvenience standing between them and more profit.

And even if this were only sentimental, after 31 years, would that really deserve so little respect?

Do you remember when we were kids and Papa let you sleep in the little room at the back where he kept the flour sacks? You loved it back there. That is part of this building too. I am not bringing it up to say we must keep everything frozen forever because of Papa and Maman. I am bringing it up because it is the same place. It was part of both our lives before it became a listing with a commission attached to it.

I am not saying you can never sell your half. I am saying that you cannot treat me as though I do not exist while you do it.

So here is what I want, plainly.

Take the building off the market this week. Stop the marketing, the photographs, and any visits until you and I have spoken and agreed on a process. No more strangers entering my bakery without notice and without my permission. We work there early in the morning. It is an operating business, not an empty property waiting for an agent to show it.

If you are determined to sell your half, then at the very least give me a genuine first opportunity to buy it. Put it in writing, with a reasonable amount of time for me to arrange financing and respond to a real offer. I am not asking you to give me the building or accept an unfair price. I am asking for a fair chance before you sell my future to somebody else. We can use an independent valuation and proper professional advice. But I cannot compete fairly against a sale process that you started in secret.

I also want you to explain why the photographer believed I had agreed. If that came from you, say so. If the agent misunderstood something, then you need to correct it immediately. And I want to know when you decided that “we decide together” no longer applied.

Then call me yourself.

Not a text. Not a message from your wife. Not another explanation through the agent. I am not trying to exclude her from decisions between you and her, but this particular conversation is between you and me. You made the promise to me after Maman’s funeral, and you are the one who needs to answer for what has happened since.

Please do not force this into lawyers and a family war. I will protect my bakery, my employees, and my interest in the building if I have to, but that is not where I want this to go. I would rather we argue directly and honestly than continue like this.

I am furious with you, but I do not hate you. You are still my brother. That is why this hurts as much as it does. It is not only the possibility of losing the bakery. It is discovering that you could make a decision affecting my whole working life and not even think I deserved a phone call.

I am still willing to talk. Do not confuse that with being calm. I am not calm. But I am willing to listen if you finally speak to me directly and take real steps to fix this.

Take the listing down this week, stop the visits, and call me yourself. That is where this starts.

[Your name]
